title: B-R-K
hook: bracha (blessing), berech (knee), breichah (pool): blessing bends and flows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-L-M: shalom, shalem, shilem. Your line was peace is wholeness. Did you pay your small debt? Today, the root under baruch, and the end of the week. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

Evening, outside a town, at a well. A servant has walked a long way with ten camels, sent to find a wife for his master's son. Before he asks anything of anyone, he brings the camels down onto their knees beside the water. In Hebrew, the verb for making them kneel is built on bet, resh, kaf, the same three letters as baruch, the first word of a blessing. Camels folding down on their knees, at a well, at dusk. Only then does the servant pray. The root of blessing, down in the dust beside the water.
screen: `A WELL AT EVENING.` → `THE CAMELS KNEEL.` → `THE SAME LETTERS AS BARUCH.`

segments.voice: B-R-K. Turn it four ways. First, bracha: a blessing. Baruch, blessed, from three days ago, grows from these letters. Second, berech: a knee. In Psalm 95, the call to worship says "let us kneel before the LORD," and the Hebrew for kneel is from this root. And in the Amidah, the standing prayer, a custom traced to the Talmud has people bend the knees at baruch, bow at atah, and stand straight again for God's name. The body says the word. Third, breichah: a pool. Water gathered low, where the ground bends down to hold it. Dictionaries list the knee and the blessing under the same letters. Whether they began as one word is a question for linguists. But some readers hear them together: blessing is something you bend toward, and something that pools and flows. Fourth, the week behind you. It began with dots, the nikud that give letters a voice. Then your first word, shalom. Then the Shema's first two words, a silent eye and a dot that moved. Then baruch atah, the opening of a blessing. Then shoresh, the root under the word, and the first root, sh-l-m, peace as wholeness. And now b-r-k, the root under the blessing you learned to read three days ago. A week ago these were single letters. Now they're words you can sound out, and roots you can dig up.
screen: `BRACHA: A BLESSING.` · `BERECH: THE KNEE THAT BENDS.` · `BREICHAH: WATER GATHERED LOW.` · `THE WEEK: DOTS, WORDS, ROOTS.` · then, large: `BLESSING BENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bend your knee in thanks. If you're able, stand. If you're sitting, that's fine too. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing from this week you're grateful for. Something small and real. Now, slowly, let your knees bend, just a little, the way the custom bends at baruch. Then straighten, and stand tall again. If you're seated, let your head bow instead, and lift it. Once is enough. Then sit, and let the thanks pool. If you pray, you can say baruch atah as you bend. The bell holds the time.
B-R-K. Bet, resh, kaf: the root of bracha, blessing, sitting beside berech, knee, and breichah, pool. Today's word.
Your line: blessing bends. Today, when you bend down for something, to tie a shoe or pick something up, let it be a small thank you. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In the Amidah, worshippers bend the knees at the word baruch, bow at atah, and straighten before God's name; the Hebrew words for blessing and knee are listed under the same three letters, b-r-k.

notes: Psalms 95:6 fragment quoted as JPS 1917 (KJV has the same words); nivrechah from B-R-K. Confirm.
Genesis 24:10–11 paraphrased: Abraham's servant, ten camels (the count is in Genesis 24:10), makes them kneel (vayavrech) by the well at evening; then prays (24:12). Confirm.
Amidah bowing custom traced to Berakhot 12a–b (bow at baruch, straighten at the Name); the knee-bend at baruch and bow at atah are the common practice. Confirm the source and phrasing.
Whether bracha and berech are etymologically one root is left open on purpose ('a question for linguists'). Script says 'some readers hear them together'.
Breichah: e.g. 2 Kings 20:20; not cited in the voice. Confirm gloss 'pool'.
Week end (days 1352–1358): the teach looks back on nikud, shalom, Shema Yisrael, baruch atah, shoresh, Sh-L-M. Callbacks say 'three days ago' rather than a weekday.

Editor pass: replaced the hook's stock close ('an odd place... or maybe exactly the right one') with a concrete image; changed 'a week ago these were shapes' to 'single letters', since the alphabet days came before this week.
